Martin Heidegger. A German philosopher from 1889 to 1976 who radically transformed the study of Being and human existence through phenomenology and existential analysis. His monumental work Being and Time, published in 1927, made questions about the meaning of Being central to philosophy and introduced the concept of authentic existence as liberation from social conformity. Though his collaboration with Nazism remains deeply controversial, his philosophical innovations profoundly influenced existentialism, hermeneutics, and continental philosophy.

His central question is deceptively simple: What does it mean to be? This reframes ontology from an abstract metaphysical puzzle into an urgent inquiry into human existence. Heidegger developed the term Dasein—being-there—as his name for human existence, emphasizing that we are always already embedded in a world of practical concerns and meanings. We do not stand outside the world observing it; we are thrown into it.

He introduced the distinction between authentic and inauthentic existence. Authentic being requires owning our freedom and mortality, rather than hiding in social convention and the "they-self" that absorbed in anonymous public life. He was a pioneer of phenomenology, the method of carefully analyzing the structures of lived experience and consciousness. He introduced the concept of thrownness, from the German Geworfenheit. We find ourselves cast into a world we did not choose, with circumstances we did not select. We must make choices, but we never choose the situation into which we are thrown.

Heidegger emphasized mood and anxiety as fundamental to human existence. Anxiety reveals our freedom and the groundlessness of our choices. We cannot find a solid foundation for our decisions. He developed hermeneutics, the study of interpretation, arguing that all understanding is fundamentally interpretive. We cannot access a meaning-independent reality; all understanding involves interpretation shaped by our situation.

Being and Time became foundational to existentialism, profoundly influencing Sartre, Camus, and later continental philosophy. Later in his career, Heidegger explored technology, which he called Technik, as a mode of revealing that risks reducing nature and humanity to mere resources to be exploited. His Nazi party membership from 1933 to 1945 remains a tragic and contested chapter. Scholars continue to debate whether his philosophy enabled fascism or was corrupted by it.
